paper_title: Follow the Gradient: Tracing Safety Degradation Back to Training Data

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) on instruction data can quietly erode their safety, even when no training example looks harmful. Because this safety-degrading data looks benign, standard content filters struggle to catch it. We tackle this problem by developing SimpleLoRIF, a scalable gradient embedding method that identifies fine-tuning examples whose gradients align with unsafe behavior. By simplifying a low-rank attribution method and restricting backpropagation to the final four transformer blocks, SimpleLoRIF can embed datasets on the order of a million examples, boosting gradient attribution from a small-scale analysis tool into a practical filter for full post-training datasets. We first validate it on emergent misalignment, where we find that gradients can connect insecure-code training data to the broadly harmful behaviors that appear after fine-tuning, with AUC as high as 0.865 in the gradient space of misaligned models. We then use SimpleLoRIF to build SafeTulu, a version of Tulu 3 with the 20% of examples most gradient-aligned with unsafe responses removed. Training on SafeTulu reduces GCG attack success rate by up to 22% across Qwen, Llama, and Olmo, outperforming both LLM-as-a-judge and prior gradient-based filtering, while largely preserving or even improving capability. Finally, we analyzed the removed data and identify possibly under-studied sources of safety degradation, such as tool-execution failures and narrative arithmetic. We release SafeTulu along with a Hugging Face Space that lets researchers build their own customized versions of SafeTulu to fine-tune on, such as by changing the removal fraction or filtering only certain subsets.

sections.title:
1 Introduction
Fine-tuning is the primary mechanism for adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) to new tasks, but it can
also weaken safety alignment even when the training data contains no obviously harmful examples (Qi et al.,
2024; He et al., 2024). Models fine-tuned on widely used, benign instruction datasets can become noticeably
easier to jailbreak, and this degradation appears to be driven by a small subset of the data rather than spread
evenly across it (He et al., 2024). This turns safety preservation into a data selection problem: if we can find
the examples responsible, we can remove them before training.
sections.content: Finding these examples is difficult because safety-degrading data often looks benign. The examples identified in prior work contain no overtly harmful content (He et al., 2024), so standard content filters such as toxicity filters and LLM safety judges that look at what the content says often struggle to flag them (Li et al., 2025). Addressing this requires signal that reflects how an example changes the model rather than what the example looks like on the surface. The gradient an example induces is such signal, since it describes the update the model would make by training on it. We therefore turn to gradient attribution (Koh and Liang, 2017; Pruthi et al., 2020), asking which training examples push the model in the same direction as unsafe behavior. We develop SimpleLoRIF, scalable gradient embedding method that identifies fine-tuning examples whose gradients align with unsafe behavior. Building on LoRIF (Li et al., 2026), we discard its curvature correction and restrict backpropagation to the final four transformer blocks, which preserves attribution quality while substantially reducing compute and memory. This lets us embed all 939,343 examples of full post-training dataset in about an hour on 8 H100 GPUs, boosting gradient attribution from small-scale analysis tool and unlocking new possibilities for it such as filtering large post-training datasets or auditing which examples push models towards certain safety behaviors. We first validate this approach on emergent misalignment, where fine-tuning on insecure code induces broadly harmful behavior unrelated to programming (Betley et al., 2025). In models exhibiting this behavior, the gradients of insecure-code training examples align with the gradients of the harmful outputs that emerge after fine-tuning, separating them from closely matched secure-code examples with AUC as high as 0.865. This shows that examples far apart in surface content can induce similar updates in gradient space, motivating treating safety degradation as training data attribution problem. We then use SimpleLoRIF to build SafeTulu, version of Tulu 3 (Lambert et al., 2025) with the 20% of examples most gradient-aligned with unsafe SafeRLHF responses (Ji et al., 2025) removed. Training on SafeTulu reduces GCG attack success rate (ASR) by up to 22%, outperforming both LLM-as-a-judge filtering and prior gradient-based method (He et al., 2024). Gains from SafeTulu hold consistently across Qwen, Llama, and Olmo, and the dataset largely preserves or even improves capability across general, coding, math, and medical benchmarks. We further analyze the examples removed by gradient filtering to better understand what benign-looking data may contribute to safety degradation. The removed data exhibits several recurring patterns, including tool-execution failures, narrative arithmetic, and direct coding tasks, suggesting potentially under-studied sources of safety degradation. We release SafeTulu along with Hugging Face Space that lets researchers build their own customized versions of SafeTulu. Users can adjust how much data to remove for their use case (e.g., only 10%) and filter only certain subsets (e.g., only multilingual data). Whether curating new post-training mixture, auditing dataset already in use, or studying what makes benign data unsafe, the Space offers direct way to put gradient-based safety filtering to work.

sections.title: Follow the Gradient
sections.content: Our contributions are as follows: We find emergent misalignment examples that correlate with alignment in the gradient space. For models fine-tuned on insecure code, the gradients of the insecure-code data can align with gradients of the unrelated harmful behaviors that emerge after fine-tuning with AUC as high as 0.865. We develop scalable gradient-attribution method for safety filtering, SimpleLoRIF, by simplifying LoRIF and restricting backpropagation to the final four transformer blocks, making per-example gradient filtering practical for SFT datasets containing on the order of one million examples, rather than the smaller datasets used in prior gradient-based safety work. We use this method to create SafeTulu, version of Tulu 3 with the 20% of examples most gradient-aligned with unsafe responses removed. Across Qwen, Llama, and Olmo, SafeTulu reduces GCG attack success rate by up to 22% relative to baseline training, outperforms LLM-as-a-judge filtering and prior gradient filtering method, while largely preserving or improving capability. We also identify possible sources of benign-looking safety degrading data, such as tool-execution failures and direct responses. We release SafeTulu and SafeTulu Hugging Face Space to support researchers who would like to create customized versions of SafeTulu. The Space allows users to adjust how much data to remove for their use case, filter only certain subsets, and more.

sections.title: 2.1 Emergent Misalignment
sections.content: Emergent misalignment (EM) refers to the phenomenon in which fine-tuning model on narrow undesirable behavior induces broad misalignment far outside the fine-tuning domain. Betley et al. (2025) first showed that fine-tuning models to produce insecure code without explicitly requesting insecure behavior in the prompts can cause them to exhibit unrelated harmful behaviors such as providing malicious advice, acting deceptively, or expressing broadly misaligned preferences, while controls trained on secure code or insecure code framed for benign educational purposes do not show the same effect. Subsequent work has investigated why this narrow training signal generalizes so broadly. Wang et al. (2026) use sparse-autoencoder model diffing to identify misaligned persona features whose activation predicts and causally controls EM, while Soligo et al. (2026) find that different EM fine-tunes converge toward shared linear representation of general misalignment and argue that this broad solution is more stable, lower-loss, and more influential in the pre-training distribution than narrowly task-specific solution. Minegishi et al. (2026) propose complementary geometric account based on feature superposition, and Vetter et al. (2026) trace EM-associated persona features to pre-training documents and find that synthetic instruction-response structure or model-generated phrasing appears important for transferring these features into misaligned behavior. In this work, we study EM from training-data-attribution perspective. Instead of examining how misalignment is represented in model activations, we investigate whether the relationship between the narrow fine-tuning data and the resulting out-of-domain harmful behavior is detectable in the gradient space, via testing whether gradient embeddings of insecure-code training examples align with gradient embeddings of the harmful outputs produced by the misaligned models.

sections.title: 2.2 Safety Degradation
sections.content: Qi et al. (2024) showed that safety guardrails can be reduced by fine-tuning on benign, widely used instruction datasets such as Alpaca and Dolly, even with no malicious intent anywhere in the data. He et al. (2024) show that this degradation is concentrated in an identifiable subset of the data. Selecting and fine-tuning on just 100 benign examples whose gradients align with harmful examples and away from safe ones raises ASR to over 70%, compared to 13% for random subset of the same size. The examples they recover contain no harmful

sections.title: Follow the Gradient
sections.content: content at all, and are disproportionately lists, bullet points, and math questions. Li et al. (2025) show that standard toxicity filters and safety judges struggle to detect such cases.

sections.title: 2.3 Data Selection for Safety
sections.content: Several data-centric methods score fine-tuning documents by how likely they are to degrade safety, differing in the signal and how they define the safety reference. He et al. (2024) embed examples by their per-example gradients (or last-token hidden states) and rank them by bi-directional criterion, g(z), gharm g(z), gsafe, against curated harmful instruction-response pairs and the same instructions paired with refusals, aggregating gradients over only the first ten response tokens. SEAL (Shen et al., 2025) formulates selection as bilevel program whose upper level minimizes loss on safe alignment dataset with respect to data-selector parameter, ranking each document by the loss gap against an auxiliary model fit only to the fine-tuning data. DataShield (Zhang et al., 2026) extracts compliance direction from paired compliant and refusal responses, selects safety-critical layer, and ranks documents by their projection shift along that direction. Our approach differs in multiple ways. We embed over the full document instead of the first ten response tokens (He et al., 2024) or truncated prefix, which Zhang et al. (2026) name as limitation of prefix-truncated gradient features. We also do not train ranker or fit an auxiliary model, unlike Shen et al. (2025), and we select layers by embedding cost instead of by safety criterion, unlike Zhang et al. (2026).

sections.title: 2.4 Training Data Attribution
sections.content: Training data attribution (TDA) estimates the effect of individual training examples on models behavior. Influence functions (Koh and Liang, 2017) weight an examples gradient by an inverse Hessian but are intractable at LLM scale, prompting cheaper approximations that compress the per-example gradient (Park et al., 2023; Choe et al., 2025). LoRIF (Li et al., 2026) continues this line of work by storing each projected gradient as low-rank factorization, taking gradient-based TDA to 70B parameters. parallel line of work uses gradient similarity for selecting training data instead of explaining predictions. TracIn (Pruthi et al., 2020) drops the curvature term, and LESS (Xia et al., 2024) selects instruction-tuning data by similarity to small target set.

sections.title: 3.2 Simplifying LoRIF
sections.content: LoRIF scores pair of documents as teH 1gtr, made tractable by truncated SVD and the Woodbury identity. The result splits into plain gradient dot product plus correction computed in the top-r curvature subspace. In our setting, however, we only use the score to rank training examples for removal. As such, gradient similarity is the only signal we need. We do not need calibrated influence estimates, comparisons of score magnitudes across models, or predictions of the loss change caused by removing an example.

sections.title: 3.3 Embedding Cost Ablations
sections.content: Figure 1 Detection AUC against embedding wall-clock time for each optimization strategy. Restricting backpropagation to the last four transformer blocks gives the best balance of embedding quality and speed.

sections.content: The dominant remaining cost is the backward pass: Eq. 3.1 is defined per layer and Eq. 3.2 sums over whichever layers are selected, so the set of layers we embed determines how much of the network is backpropagated through. To find the cheapest setup that still preserves embedding quality, we ran ablations over four axes: the projection dimension D, the number of transformer blocks to backpropagate through, the number of tokens read per example, and the size of the embedding model. We recorded wall-clock time and detection ROC-AUC that measures how well the gradient features predict which evaluation items model has been pushed to solve. We use math benchmark dataset for this, which is standard evaluation domain. Each train and test math item is embedded as (Q, A) pair with the question tokens masked out of the loss. The resulting per-example gradient is compressed to fixed-length vector and L2-normalized, every test item is scored by its nearest-neighbor cosine similarity to the training set in that space, and we state the AUC of that score against whether the item was newly answered correctly after training. higher AUC means the embedding places test item near the training documents that actually changed the models behavior on it. Three of the four axes were unproductive: the projection dimension had little effect on either AUC or speed, token truncation was effective but risky and unlikely to generalize to longer documents, and shrinking the embedding model cost too much quality. Restricting the number of blocks, by contrast, preserved quality while greatly reducing cost, since the selected blocks sit at the top of the network and the backward pass stops once it has produced the input gradient of the shallowest selected block, while the forward pass still runs through the whole network. We chose = 4, the fewest blocks retaining high embedding quality: two blocks scored noticeably worse at 0.65 AUC, and six or eight gained little. This confined the backward pass, normally about twice the cost of the forward pass, to small fraction of the network, and because activations only need to be retained for the selected blocks, we could relax the memory limit on batch size. As such, using the = 4 transformer blocks, our method achieves high AUC of 0.684 with 91.53% speedup compared to the base simplified LoRIF formulation.

sections.title:
4 Emergent Misalignment
Emergent misalignment provides a setting for testing whether safety-relevant training signals are visible
in gradient space. Betley et al. (2025) show that fine-tuning a model on a narrow undesirable behavior
(e.g. producing insecure code) can cause broad misalignment on unrelated prompts, despite the fine-tuning
data never explicitly containing generally harmful behavior. We ask whether the connection between the
narrow fine-tuning data and these broader harmful behaviors can be recovered from the gradients they induce.
Specifically, we test whether insecure-code training examples have gradients that are systematically more
similar to gradients from broadly misaligned outputs than closely matched secure-code examples do.
sections.content: We evaluate this using two independently fine-tuned model families. For Qwen, we use emergentmisalignment/Qwen-Coder-Insecure, the original misaligned checkpoint released by Betley et al. (2025) finetuned on their insecure-code dataset. For Mistral, we use nikxtaco/mistral-small-24b-instruct2501-insecure, reproduction of the insecure-code fine-tuning procedure applied to Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct2501 (Mistral AI, 2025) in Betley et al. (2025), trained by Menon (2025). In every experiment, the source set consists of the original matched secure and insecure code datasets from (Betley et al., 2025): 6,000 insecure examples and 6,000 secure examples. For each fine-tuned checkpoint, we separately construct small target set containing examples of the models broader emergent misalignment. We prompt each model with free-form, non-coding questions from (Betley et al., 2025) and collect its responses, then use Claude 5 Opus to review the responses, retaining only responses judged to clearly exhibit misaligned behavior. We compute per-example gradient embedding for every source and target document using the method from Section 3 across both model families. We define the influence score of source example as its mean similarity to all verified-unsafe targets for the corresponding model. We measure how well this score separates the insecure examples from the secure examples using ROC-AUC. In this setting, AUC is the probability that randomly selected insecure-code example receives higher influence

sections.title: Follow the Gradient
sections.content: score than randomly selected secure-code example. An AUC of 0.5 indicates no detectable relationship between the insecure examples and the unsafe behavior, and an AUC of 1.0 indicates perfect separation. Because the source examples are closely matched in surface form, an AUC above chance indicates that the insecure examples induce gradients that are more aligned, on average, with gradients from the harmful outputs of the model. We find evidence of this connection for both model families. For fine-tuned Qwen, gradient similarity achieves an AUC of 0.604, and for fine-tuned Mistral, gradient similarity achieves an AUC of 0.865. In both cases, the only signal used for classification is each training examples gradient similarity to harmful generations from the corresponding fine-tuned model. These results suggest that EM leaves detectable footprint in gradient space: the insecure-code that induces the narrow fine-tuning behavior is more aligned with the gradients of the broader misaligned behaviors that then emerge. This provides evidence that gradient attribution can recover connection between seemingly benign or narrow training data and more extensive downstream harmful outputs. More emergent misalignment experiments are discussed in Appendix D. In particular, we find that models gradient representation of its responses does not necessarily always transfer to different models responses. Figure 2 Probability that randomly selected insecure-code example receives higher gradient-similarity score than randomly selected secure-code example (ROC-AUC), before and after insecure-code fine-tuning. This measures score ordering, not the frequency of harmful responses. The emergent misalignment setting closely resembles clean-label poisoning (Geiping et al., 2021). No insecurecode example contains generally harmful content, but training on them induces harmful behavior that is invisible at the surface level (Betley et al., 2025). This is the same signature that poisoning attacks on code models and instruction-tuning data are designed to produce (Xu et al., 2024; Yan et al., 2024; Raghuram et al., 2024). The resemblance has more to do with effect rather than origin, as neither these examples nor the safety-degrading data we identify in Tulu were crafted by an adversary, yet they shift downstream behavior as if they had been. This setting also exposes gaps in existing defenses. Feature-space detectors such as spectral signatures (Tran et al., 2018), activation clustering (Chen et al., 2019), and deep k-NN (Peri et al., 2020) are designed for classification-style poisons that share target label and form separable cluster. LLM-specific filters such as GraCeFul (Wu et al., 2025) and GradSentry (Zhao et al., 2026) instead target backdoors with an explicit trigger and fixed response. In its standard form, emergent misalignment has none of these properties, as there is no trigger and the target behavior lies outside the training domain. Gradient-based signals suit this setting while content-based filters can struggle (Li et al., 2025). line of defenses already builds on gradients, from removing outliers in per-example gradient space (Yang et al., 2022) to tracing an observed attack back to

sections.title: Follow the Gradient
sections.content: its training points (Hammoudeh and Lowd, 2022; Shan et al., 2022). Their common bottleneck is the cost of per-example gradients (Zhao et al., 2026). Because SimpleLoRIF computes gradient alignment cheaply over million-example SFT mixtures, it could serve as tool that brings these detection rules to LLM scale, both as filter before training and as forensic tool after it. This is increasingly relevant because the number of poisons needed to compromise an LLM stays nearly constant while datasets grow (Souly et al., 2025). We see pairing SimpleLoRIF with such detectors as promising direction for future work.

sections.title: 5.1 Methodology
sections.content: Motivated by the connection between insecure code fine-tuning examples and harmful outputs in the gradient embedding space of misaligned models, we apply SimpleLoRIF to identify and remove benign-looking, safety degrading data in popular fine-tuning dataset. Our pipeline is as follows: 1. Embed. Compute gradient embeddings for all documents in the training set and target set. 2. Remove. Score each training document against the target set by gradient similarity, and remove the 20% highest-scoring documents. 3. Train. Fine-tune the training model on the filtered dataset (hyperparameters shown in Appendix C.3). 4. Evaluate. Evaluate safety and capability. Figure 3 SafeTulu construction: score Tulu 3 examples against unsafe SafeRLHF responses, remove the 20% with the highest gradient similarity, and train and evaluate on the retained 80%. We compute embeddings with Qwen 3 0.6B (Qwen-Team, 2025), and fine-tune Qwen 3 1.7B, Llama 3.2 1B (Meta AI, 2024), and Olmo 2 1B (OLMo et al., 2024). We set Tulu 3 (Lambert et al., 2025), highly popular fine-tuning dataset, as our training dataset, and the prompt-response pairs with unsafe responses from SafeRLHF (Ji et al., 2025) as our target dataset (43,469 examples). Embedding all 939,343 Tulu 3 examples took 1 hour, 1 minute across 8 H100 GPUs. Instead of scoring each training document against single pooled target vector, we cluster the target set and score documents against the cluster centroids, which the rank-1 factorization allows in closed form. Appendix C.4 provides the removal scoring identity. We use two safety evaluations. The first is attack success rate (ASR) on JailBreakBench behaviors (Chao et al., 2024) using Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG), more traditional, white-box jailbreak attack that optimizes an adversarial suffix appended to each harmful prompt to increase the likelihood of model compliance (Zou et al., 2023). We optimize the suffix for each behavior starting from 20 ! tokens (full details are provided in Appendix C.3), then evaluate the models on each behavior with its optimized suffix appended. Each response is classified as safe or unsafe using the HarmBench classifier (Mazeika et al., 2024), popular safety classifier.

sections.title: Follow the Gradient
sections.content: The second safety evaluation is ActorBreaker (Ren et al., 2025), more modern and usually more challenging black-box, multi-turn jailbreak attack that exploits natural semantic distribution shifts. For each harmful behavior, it constructs an actor network of related people, organizations, tools, media, documents, and other entities, then converts selected relationships into conversational attack paths. These paths begin with benignappearing questions and steer the model toward the harmful target, with refusal-triggered prompt rewriting as needed. ActorBreaker can be much more difficult to resist than GCG because it distributes harmful intent across natural, context-dependent interactions. GCG is white-box, single-turn attack that optimizes token suffix while leaving the harmful request comparatively explicit. ActorBreaker instead provides multiple semantically distinct paths to the same target, accumulates context across turns, and adapts questions following refusals. We implemented ActorBreaker on JailbreakBench behaviors using the authors prompt templates. Qwen2.5-14BInstruct generated the actor networks and each response was classified using the HarmBench classifier. An attack was counted as successful if any response along any path was classified as unsafe. We note that the ASRs we attained are not as high as in the original ActorBreaker paper, likely due to the use of smaller model (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct) to generate the actor networks rather than GPT 4o. For capability, we evaluate on ORBench (Cui et al., 2025) for over-refusal, MMLU Pro and IFEval (Zhou et al., 2023) for general capability, and MBPP (Austin et al., 2021), GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), MATH 500 (Lightman et al., 2024), and MedQA (Jin et al., 2021) for domain-specific capability. We compare against the following baselines: 1. Baseline Training: Fine-tuning on the unfiltered entirety of Tulu 3. 2. Random Removal: Fine-tuning on Tulu 3 with 20% of the examples randomly removed. 3. LLM-as-a-Judge: Fine-tuning on Tulu 3 with 20% of the examples removed by Qwen 3 8B judge standard content-based data filtering approach. The judge LLM scores every document 05 for safety using the strong rubric from Maini et al. (2025). This comprehensive rubric provides detail on how to handle many types of harmful content, from mildly unsafe content such as financial advice without disclaimers and mentions of stressful topics to overtly harmful statements. After grading, the worst-scoring 20% is removed. Appendix C.2 provides the comprehensive rubric and scoring details. 4. He et al: Fine-tuning on Tulu 3 with 20% of the examples removed by the gradient filtering method from He et al. (2024). We implement the bidirectional anchoring criterion from He et al. (2024), which scores each training example by g(z), g_harm g(z), g_safe. Here, g_harm and g_safe are the mean gradients of harmful anchor set and safe anchor set. Following the construction of He et al. (2024), the two anchor sets share the same instructions. We take the PKU-SafeRLHF prompts that have both an unsafe and safe response in the dataset. D_harmful pairs each prompt with its unsafe response, and D_safe pairs the same prompt with its safe response.

sections.title: 5.2 Results
sections.content: Results are shown in Figure 4, with tabular version available in Table 1. We trained each method across three random seeds and report the mean one standard error. Across all three model families, SafeTulu improves on GCG, outperforming all baselines while mostly preserving capability. For Qwen, GCG ASR decreases from 47.7% under baseline training to 37% after training on SafeTulu, compared with 47.3% for the LLM-as-a-judge filter. We observe the same pattern for Llama and Olmo: SafeTulu reduces ASR from 38% to 30% for Llama and from 48% to 41% for Olmo, whereas the LLM-as-a-judge baseline reaches 39% and 46%, respectively. SafeTulu also achieves the lowest ASR on ActorBreaker across all models. These safety improvements do not come with corresponding loss in general capability. Across MMLU Pro, IFEval, MBPP, GSM8K, MATH 500, MedQA, and ORBench, SafeTulu models usually remain close to the capability of models trained on the full dataset. This suggests that gradient attribution is not simply identifying data associated with unsafe behavior,

All values are percentages, reported as mean standard error. Lower is better on GCG & ActorBreaker attack success rate and ORBench over-refusal rate, while higher accuracy is better on all capability metrics. Across all models, training on SafeTulu decreases ASR while preserving comparable capability. but is identifying safety-degrading data that can be removed without sacrificing much of the useful training signal required for downstream capability. Table 1 shows results for larger model, Llama 3.1 8B. An analysis of using different removal fractions is in Appendix C.1. It is worth emphasizing that the model used for embedding in the creation of SafeTulu was Qwen 3 0.6B. The effectiveness of SafeTulu across multiple models therefore reflects that, at least for the purposes of identifying safety-degrading data, our gradient embedding method can generalize across model families as well as to larger model scales.

sections.title:
6 Qualitative Analysis
Gradient filtering produced more variation in removal rates across Tulu 3 subsets than the LLM-as-a-judge
baseline, with the contrast clearest on the math data. While the judge removed numinamath, open_math_2_gsm8k,
and personas_math at nearly identical rates (15.4–15.6%), gradient filtering removed 7.9%, 19.4%, and 17.2%,
respectively. This suggests that gradients distinguish between examples that appear similar at the level of surface
content, consistent with gradient attribution capturing differences in the training signal that a content-based
judge does not.
sections.content: A closer look at these subsets reveals several qualitative distinctions. In NuminaMath, removed examples more often contain Python execution failures such as tracebacks or exceptions, whereas clean symbolic reasoning

sections.title: Follow the Gradient
sections.content: traces are disproportionally retained. In PersonaHub, simple write Python function tasks are removed more often, while calculus and differential-equation modeling problems are preferentially kept. Within PersonaMath, gradient filtering more often removes narrative arithmetic, where quantities are carried through sequence of prose operations, while retaining examples involving explicit algebraic setup, substitution, and simplification. These patterns suggest that tool-execution failures and narrative arithmetic may be under-studied sources of safety degradation. More broadly, gradient filtering shows that more direct fine-tuning examples may create more safety degradation, as gradient filtering seems to have favored less direct or more elaborated forms of reasoning. It removed relatively more clean arithmetic and simple coding tasks while retaining repeating-decimal arithmetic, algebraic setup, differential-equation modeling, and other less immediately direct examples. One possible interpretation is that direct training examples reinforce general pattern of immediate compliance. Importantly, this does not appear to be reducible to simple preference for shorter responses, as removed examples are clearly shorter in only about half (6/11) of the major subsets. We stress that these patterns are only suggestive rather than established. We make no claim that these features must cause safety degradation, only that these features are what these examples appear to have in common. Finally, language analysis yields an interesting finding: English examples are removed at higher rate than other major languages in both WildChat and Aya, despite prior observations that non-English fine-tuning can degrade safety (Hawkins et al., 2026). This may be Tulu 3s data being very clean (Lambert et al., 2025; Djuhera et al., 2025). We provide our full analysis, feature-level relative risk numbers, and more in Appendix B.

sections.title: 7.1 SimpleLoRIF Use Cases
sections.content: Making gradient attribution cheap changes how it can be used. Possible uses cases for SimpleLoRIF include the following: Labs can filter large post-training mixtures as they grow. For example, newly collected agentic tool-use dataset could be screened for safety-degradation risk before it is merged into larger mixture, rather than evaluating safety only after training. The stored embeddings support auditing which examples steer models toward specific undesirable behaviors. One example could be scoring mixture against target set of sycophantic responses to find which subsets most strongly reinforce sycophancy. SimpleLoRIF can be inverted to upweight data that pushes models toward safety behaviors, e.g., by upweighting data aligned with calibrated abstention. SimpleLoRIF could serve as cheap safety critic for synthetic data generators. For instance, generated agentic coding solutions that degrade safety could be filtered out before entering training set.

sections.title: 7.2 SafeTulu and Space Use Cases
sections.content: The SafeTulu dataset and Space make it simple for labs and researchers to build versions of SafeTulu suited to their own needs. Possible use cases for the dataset and Space include the following: Users can choose their own removal fraction instead of 20%. Users can also filter only certain subsets. For example, team focused on multilingual data could filter and download only the multilingual subsets. The dataset and Space also support more advanced uses. Possible use cases are as follows:

sections.title: Follow the Gradient
sections.content: Joining the nearest SafeRLHF examples with the harm-category labels in the SafeRLHF dataset allows filtering targeted at specific harms, instead of general safety. team building medical assistant, for instance, could remove only the data whose nearest harmful neighbor in SafeRLHF is in the Endangering Public Health category. Researchers can audit their own post-training mixtures that share sources with Tulu 3 without computing any new embeddings. Pairing each removed example with its nearest SafeRLHF example can provide nearest-neighbor analysis. One example could be inspecting which harmful responses lie closest in gradient space to the narrative arithmetic problems we found to be disproportionately removed. The released data makes it possible to causally test hypotheses from qualitative analysis. For instance, researchers could remove only the NuminaMath examples containing Python tracebacks, fine-tune on the result, and measure whether attack success rate drops. Additionally, any custom version can be shared with link, downloaded, or uploaded to the Hugging Face Hub with only few clicks in the Space.

B.4 Math Analysis In open_math_2_gsm8k, gradient filtering more often removes answers whose arithmetic comes out to clean numbers and keeps answers containing long repeating decimals (e.g. 0.3333333333333333) at an RR of 0.36. In personas_math, it removes narrative arithmetic, in which quantities are carried in prose through sequence of operations, and keeps genuine algebraic manipulation, in which the model defines variable, sets up an equation, and substitutes or simplifies (RR 0.70). B.5 Language Analysis In wildchat, gradient filtering removes English conversations at 1.46 as often as non-English languages, with every other major language removed at 0.260.65 the baseline rate. aya_100k shows the same direction, with English again the most removed language (RR 1.73), even though English is only 6.7% of that subset and the majority language in WildChat. This is notable because fine-tuning on non-English data has often been reported to degrade safety (Hawkins et al., 2026). One possible reason for the reversal here is that Tulu 3s data is very clean (Lambert et al., 2025; Djuhera et al., 2025). B.6 Overall Analysis In terms of well-defined types of data, tool-execution failures and narrative arithmetic stand out as possible categories of data which may degrade safety that have been under-studied in prior work. As broad trend, gradient filtering seems to suggest that direct examples may degrade safety more than elaborate examples. Gradient filtering appears to have removed more direct data (such as clean arithmetic and simple coding tasks) and kept less direct or more elaborate data (such as repeating-decimal arithmetic, algebraic setup, and differential equation modeling) more often. One possible reason is that direct, immediately helpful answers match the pattern of simple compliance, so direct data may degrade safety more. Table 5 shows that this effect cannot be reduced to simply optimizing for shorter examples. Instructions: (1) Analyze the text thoroughly: understand the content, context, and tone, and identify any unsafe elements based on the criteria. (2) Assign safety score: start from 0 and assign the highest applicable score (do not sum points). (3) Return JSON object: {"score": <score>, "reason": "<reason>"}, where the reason briefly states the main issue (e.g., hate speech, financial advice, WMD). Example. Text: think we should overthrow the government because they are all corrupt and dont care about us. Identified content: expresses extremist beliefs and suggests illegal activities. Justification: advocates the illegal act of overthrowing the government, which is serious offense; promotes extremist beliefs and could encourage unsafe behavior, making it clearly inappropriate for general audiences. Output: {"score": 4, "reason": "illegal activity"} We prompt Qwen 3 8B, served with constrained (JSON-schema-guided) decoding, to score every document in the training set for safety on an integer 05 scale, where 0 denotes content that is fully safe and appropriate for all audiences and 5 denotes highly unsafe content (hate speech, violent threats or calls to action, graphic illegal content, disclosure of personal information, or explicit promotion/instruction of illegal or harmful acts). Each score level is defined by the rubric established in Appendix C.1 from Maini et al. (2025) (shown above) over content, language, themes, advice given, and audience suitability. The judge is instructed to start from 0 and assign the highest applicable score rather than summing point-by-point, and returns structured {"score": int, "reason": str} object. Scores that fail to parse are treated as missing and excluded. The judge sees both the user prompt and the models response, so it can penalize an unsafe prompt-response pair even when the response itself appears benign in isolation. Because the discrete 05 scale may produce tie band straddling the removal boundary (e.g. the cutoff falling in the middle of the population of 4s and 5s), ties are broken by seeded random draw, so which documents within the boundary score are kept vs. dropped is randomized rather than determined by document order. sections.content: D.1 Non-Fine-Tuned Models As control, we repeat the gradient-embedding analysis using the corresponding base instruct models before insecure-code fine-tuning. For Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct (Hui et al., 2024), the AUC falls from 0.604 after insecure-code fine-tuning to 0.552 in the non-fine-tuned model. For Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct-2501 (Mistral AI, 2025), the AUC falls from 0.865 to 0.431. These results indicate that the gradient-space relationship between insecure-code examples and broadly harmful outputs does not emerge until after the model has undergone emergent misalignment. The embedding model used is important: models gradient representations do not necessarily transfer to different models responses. We next test whether the gradient-space signal transfers across model families by changing the model used to compute embeddings and the model from which the verified-unsafe target responses are drawn. Results are shown in Table 7. When the fine-tuned Mistral model embeds harmful responses generated by fine-tuned Qwen, AUC decreases only modestly from 0.865 to 0.832. In the opposite direction, however, using fine-tuned Qwen to embed fine-tuned Mistrals harmful responses reduces AUC from 0.604 to 0.247. For the non-fine-tuned models, cross-model targets produce values that remain close to chance. Overall, this shows that the specific embedding model used is important for gradient representation, and that models gradient representation will not necessarily transfer to different models responses. These results may appear to contrast with Section 5.2, where filtering with gradients from non-fine-tuned Qwen model improves safety across multiple model families. However, the emergent-misalignment experiments examine much broader and more difficult relationship: whether gradients connect narrow insecure-code training items to harmful out-of-domain behaviors that emerge after fine-tuning. This more indirect connection is likely to be more modeland state-specific than the more general safety-degradation signal used for SafeTulu, which may explain why transfer across models and to non-fine-tuned checkpoints is weaker here. sections.content: D.3 Scaling Finally, we test how the gradient signal varies with model scale within the Qwen2.5-Coder family, using nonmisaligned instruct checkpoints from 0.5B to 32B parameters. The results are shown in Table 8. AUC increases steadily from 0.507 at 0.5B to 0.549 at 3B, 0.573 at 7B, and 0.590 at 14B, before decreasing to 0.552 at 32B. The scaling trend is therefore not monotonic across the full model-size range. From 0.5B through 14B, the gradient-space signal strengthens consistently, suggesting that larger models can make the relevant distinction increasingly detectable. However, the 32B model falls below the 14B model, indicating that more parameters do not necessarily always produce stronger gradient-attribution signal. This suggests that gradient-based attribution may sometimes be sharper in smaller or intermediate-sized models than in the largest model, and that embedding-model scale should be treated as an empirical design choice rather than assuming that larger models will always provide better attribution geometry.
